speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I now deal, Mr. Chairman, with some of the other points made in the debate on second reading. The hon. member for Edmonton West went into some detail on the importance of the negotiations and the resulting legislation that is now before us. I think it is useful to remember that the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs held some 22 meetings for the purpose of studying the resolutions which are now reflected before us in Bill No. C-131. The committee heard many briefs from groups and members of the general public as well as 
evidence from government officials and ministers. I think we should keep in mind the detailed study that was given to the resolutions at that time and perhaps agree that this committee of the whole house may not feel it necessary to carry out the work that would have had to be done had the standing committee not been given the opportunity of making a detailed study of these proposals.
The hon. member for Edmonton West referred to the manner in which certain tax changes were continued in effect when the house was dissolved for an election. It is my understanding that no tax increases were kept in effect by order in council. On the contrary, Mr. Chairman, the order in council in question was put into effect for the purpose of continuing reductions in duties.
In this regard I might draw the attention of the committee to a statement made by the Minister of Finance on April 26, 1968, a statement which was issued in the form of a press release. In it the minister said that all of the proposed reductions in duties were being continued in effect by means of an order in council, under the authority of section 22 of the Financial Administration Act.
The minister did note at the time, that the budgets of June 1 and November 30, 1967 and the resolution introduced on November 6, 1967, resulted in higher customs duties on some imported products, and in line with the traditional and long-established practice followed by various governments of various political persuasions these increases had been collected on a provisional basis, pending parliamentary passage of legislation to implement them. However, he concluded his statement by saying that since the twenty seventh parliament had been dissolved before passage of the legislation in question, the Department of National Revenue was suspending the collection of the increase in customs duties effective April 24, 1968, pending action by the next parliament, and that the government would collect duties on the imports involved at the former rates.
The minister also went on to say that it was the government's intention to ask the next parliament to pass legislation implementing both the reductions and the increase, effective from the dates originally proposed in the tariff resolution submitted to the last session of parliament. This, in part, is the work that we are attempting to carry out at the present time.
I can assure this committee that the government is well aware that there may be
December 3, 19S8

problems of adjustment for certain segments of Canadian industry, and this is why it has set up the general adjustment assistance program. It should be a matter of some satisfaction that to date, out of the hundreds of general inquiries received by the board, there have only been 11 formal submissions for assistance under the program, only one of which, if I am not mistaken, was based on an allegation of injury as a result of the various changes rather than a request for assistance to enable the firm in question to take advantage of additional opportunities created by the Kennedy round tariff negotiations.
The hon. member for Edmonton West and also the hon. member for Wellington drew the attention of the committee to the importance of dealing with non-tariff barriers. I can assure the committee that the government is certainly aware of the need for further action to eliminate non-tariff barriers. When I spoke on the resolution stage I believe I mentioned a special working party, of which Canada is a member, set up under GATT to develop programs for this very purpose. The GATT countries' working party is now examining how best to deal with the non-tariff barriers that are identified by member countries and, as I have said, we are taking a very active part in these discussions.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw repeated his suggestion about keeping in constant touch with the effects of the Kennedy round changes upon the agricultural industry. I can assure the hon. member that this is a practice that is now being observed. The hon. member also made some remarks about multi-national corporations. I think this committee should be aware that the Minister of Finance, when he spoke in New York on November 18, made it clear that the government is fully aware of the problems that can be created by multinational corporations for international trade. Certainly it is giving attention to the study of measures that might be put into effect to deal with these problems.
If I may deal briefly with one or two other points, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Huron wanted to know what effect the tariff changes would have on the salt industry. I can assure him that this situation is being kept under review. Present indications seem to be reasonably optimistic. I am informed that there are at least two new developments being introduced in the method of production. I understand that an announcement was made recently of a new salt manufacturing plant in Saskatchewan. Also may I reassure him that gloves have not been affected by the Kennedy
Customs Tariff
round changes that are reflected in this bill. The tariff remains unchanged at 20 per cent British preferential, 25 per cent most favoured nation. He also made some reference to a higher duty on loading tools for shells, I believe. I am informed that changes in this matter will come about as a result of a ruling of the Tariff board rather than through any changes we are considering at this time. We are keeping this matter under review as well.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that various hon. members have made references to the possible effects of the tariff changes in question. I should therefore like to repeat again what I said when I concluded the debate on the resolution stage. Most of the changes we are considering now in the form of Bill C-131 have been in effect provisionally for almost one year, and therefore we are able to see actual results and definite trends with respect to our international trade. I think most observers will agree that the results so far are very encouraging.
I put some figures on the record when I spoke on November 19, pointing out that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, in a speech to the Canadian Export Association a few weeks ago, stated that in the first nine months of 1968 our merchandise exports reached $9.9 billion, up 1.6 billion or 18.4 per cent from the same period last year. I said:
Meanwhile our imports have risen at a slower rate, by $811 million or about 10 per cent. In consequence I think we should be pleased to note that Canada is well on its way to achieving a $1 billion merchandise trade surplus this year... this will be the largest favourable trade balance recorded in the post-war period.
All this has happened since the Kennedy round changes went into effect almost one year ago. So, although one can understand the concern and apprehension which have been expressed, I think the actual facts shown by the figures should provide not only reassurance but also encouragement as to the positive effect over all for Canada, Canadian industry and Canadian workers of the results of the tariff negotiations reflected in this bill. Therefore I would certainly urge the committee to give this bill favourable consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to direct some remarks to the parliamentary secretary following my remarks of November 14. I still wish to hear a definition of the term "internal combustion tractor". That definition ought to be included somewhere in this bill. Although the parliamentary secretary said

December 3, 1SS3
Customs Tariff
that the present wording of the resolution would have no adverse effect on farm tractors I can only say that I have dealt with the Department of National Revenue for 11 years as a farmer and I doubt that the officials of that department will take the opinion of the parliamentary secretary when it comes to defining farm tractors. I suggest that the matter should be clarified in the bill. As I said the other day, it is the duty of the Department of Finance officials to insert certain tariff items but it is the duty of Department of National Revenue officials to interpret them. Opinions on the correctness of interpretations vary. On several occasions I have had to deal with Department of National Revenue officials on a matter of interpreting terms inserted in resolutions by Department of Finance officials. I have had some experience in this field.
Frankly, I do not see how we can define an internal combustion tractor as anything but a tractor. You would have great difficulty in convincing Department of National Revenue officials that a farm tractor is not an internal combustion tractor. It is, in fact, an internal combustion machine, tractor or piece of equipment. Yet I doubt whether I could convince officials of the Department of National Revenue of the correctness of my remarks. Item 42711-1 lists:
Machines and tools, including blades, loaders, rippers, rakes and related operating and controlling gear; all the foregoing for use on internal combustion tractors-
Under item 40924-1 I am entitled to bring most of these things into the country; yet unless I show the officials of the department a copy of Hansard in five years time and allow them to read the remarks of the parliamentary secretary, there would be no way for them to know what parliament intended with regard to the definition of tractors.
A little while ago the hon. member for Kent-Essex said there is no tariff on farm machinery that is brought into this country. I know that other hon. members have made a similar statement in the past. It has been made over the years, and I can only say that it is erroneous. Everyone in Canada believes that that is the principle under which we operate; yet we do not work that way. Many farmers who have tried to bring in pieces of equipment that are covered by item 40924-1 have had a rude shock.
I received a letter from the Department of National Revenue recently. No matter whether an item says that a piece of equipment is to

be used for farm purposes only, or whether it says that the implements listed must be agricultural tools not otherwise provided for, the department makes a certain kind of finding. The minister sent me this letter which says in part:
It is the position of the department that in order to qualify as an agricultural machine an article must contain mechanical features and be recognizably "agricultural".
You will notice, Mr. Chairman, the two qualifications, "mechanical features" and "recognizably agricultural". I continue:
The Tariff Board set forth this principle in Appeal No. 237 and it has been followed by the Board on other occasions.
In other words, it must be determined at time of importation whether or not an article is an "agricultural machine". The fact that one particular unit may be for use on a farm does not in itself qualify the product as an agricultural machine.
In other words, there must be a user's certificate that the implement is to be for farm use. I continue:
Similarly, an agricultural machine may, on occasion, be for other than farm use.
I said the other night that almost any piece of agricultural machinery may have another use than a farm use. Any piece of farm machinery may be used for a purpose other than that which it was originally intended for, and we do not deny that. We think, however, that the intent of parliament is not being carried out by applying narrow definitions rigidly, since it was the intention to allow farm equipment and machinery into Canada duty free. That is not the case so far as officials of the Department of National Revenue are concerned. My letter goes on to say:
Some of the articles classified as agricultural machines are feed mixing machines, post drivers, stone pickers and transplanters. These articles are considered to be entitled to duty free entry under tariff item 40924-1 irrespective of whether they are for use by farmers or by others.
Certainly post drivers are not mechanical instruments. Other implements covered under item 40924-1 are not mechanical; yet they are allowed in duty free to be used on farms.
I wish to make a few suggestions to the parliamentary secretary who is piloting the bill through the house. He said on the 14th of November that he was in no position to accept proposals. I wonder whether he would not prefer accepting proposals to voting on amendments, since if we introduce amendments much time would be consumed.

My main interest in this bill relates to item 40924-1. When I was speaking the other night I believe I referred to equipment that is included under item 42711-1. I say there is a relation between the two. I am interested only in the clarification or interpretation of the articles listed in this entry relating to agriculture. It is my only concern with this whole bill. The difficulty has arisen because of the way in which this item was worded. It fails to portray the true intent of parliament to those who are responsible for its interpretation. This has cost the farmers of Canada many thousands of dollars in the payment of duty which parliament never intended them to pay. This affects any individual farmer who tries to bring equipment or machinery into Canada.
The suggestion has been made by officials of the Department of National Revenue that if farmers are not satisfied with the decisions reached as to duty they should appeal to the Customs Tariff Appeal Board. The last item to which I referred involved $300. If a farmer were to come to Ottawa and hire a lawyer it would certainly cost him much more than $300. This is why farmers prefer to pay than to fight these decisions. I maintain that hundreds of farmers have been obliged to pay this duty. Officials of the department, because of the power they have, can force farmers to do so even though they should not really have to meet these charges.
I can imagine what the parliamentary secretary will say after I have sat down. He will tell us he is in no position to change this item because it is related to the Kennedy round agreement. I want to tell him, as I said the other night, that this issue has been fought here for seven years to my knowledge. Former ministers have made promises similar to the one he has made-undertakings that it would be considered by various officials and taken care of. Well, the item with which I have been concerned, and in connection with which I have fought for seven years, has still not been fixed up despite promises by various ministers. This is why I intend, if possible, to propose amendments to this bill. I can tell the parliamentary secretary that what I intend to propose would not result in any change in the revenues of the department. I intend to suggest certain changes in item 40924-1.
I say that the sequence in which the items are listed is confusing to the public and confusing to the officials of the Department of National Revenue. There are 35 articles
Customs Tariff
listed under the entry, all relating, presumably, to agriculture. The 23rd states: "All the foregoing for use on the farm for farm purposes only." I have a question to ask. Why does this particular item appear only two-thirds of the way down the list? Why is it in the 23rd position? Why does it not relate to the ten items which follow it? Is there a presumption that items 1 to 22 could be used for some other purpose but that when used for farm purposes they are allowed entry duty free? What differentiates articles 1 to 22 from articles 24 to 34? I suggest that in reality there is no difference at all.
Any piece of equipment, apparatus or machinery used on a farm today can conceivably be used for some other purpose. It could, for example, be used by industry. This is no argument for the department to put up when we know what the intent of parliament is, namely, that farm machinery shall be allowed entry duty free. The department will not accept an end-user's certificate. What will it accept? Practically nothing. It is concerned only with forcing an individual farmer to pay a duty from which the law is supposed to exempt him.
There is a possibility that item 23 could have been inserted in the wrong place in the list. It could be a printer's mistake. There is also a possibility that at one time the original list only contained 23 items and that item 23 was then the last on the list. This is probably what has happened. Items 24 to 34 may have been additions consequent upon amendments to the original list. If items 24 to 34 were to be treated in the same way as all the others on the list they should have been inserted above the present item 23. There is no reason for treating them differently from the preceding items.
It seems to me that as members of this house we would be abdicating our responsibility if we did not attempt to clarify this entry. Several of us have made representations to the government time and time again, to administrations representing both parties, but no change has taken place. I have stated on many occasions that the entry as it now stands is most confusing to those responsible for its interpretation. How could it be otherwise when one department is responsible for making these lists and another is supposed to interpret what they mean? Proof of what I say can be obtained by reading various decisions of tlie Tariff Board, and letters in the possession of departmental officials.

There are several ways in which clarification could be achieved. One would be to accept the proposal I made on November 14, 1968 to change the wording of item No. 34 from "All other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery N.O.P" to "All equipment, apparatus, machines and implements N.O.P. for agricultural use." I think this is what the members of the Tariff Board want. Then again, the position of article 23, which reads "All the foregoing for use on the farm for farm purpose only" could be changed, making it the last article in the list of items.
The third proposal I wish to make is that parliament should update the terminology of some of these items. For instance, there is a reference here to wagon boxes, which are no longer used on farms. If this were changed to "truck boxes" a useful purpose would be served. I would refer also to the use of the term "sprinkler irrigation systems". This may have been the original designation, but since that time we have become familiar with such descriptions as "flood irrigation", "ditch irrigation", and so on. If a farmer tries to bring in a motor which could be used on a sprinkler system and lets out, by inadvertence, that it is for use in connection with a flood irrigation system, the department says at once: it is taxable. This shows just how narrow these decisions can get.
I believe such changes as these would bring the entry into conformity with the intention of parliament, help keep the cost of farm produce down to a minimum, and carry out in practice a principle which has been recognized by the farmers of Canada for many years, namely, that farm machinery and equipment should enter this country free of customs duty. At any rate, this is the principle which is presumably recognized. When farmers try to take advantage of it, they find it is not.
I may have some other remarks to make later if I move amendments. However, I should like to give the parliamentary secretary an opportunity to say, if he can do so, that he will have item 23 moved so as to be the last item on the list. This will not change the revenue picture one bit but will make relations with the department more definite. This would clarify it so far as I am concerned. It will give us another opportunity to go after the Department of National Revenue officials about their interpretation. They are very cautious about this. They are very contradictory at times, depending on the article you want to bring in. At one time they will

say, "If the item is of an active nature we will allow it in." At another time they will say, "If it is of a passive nature we will allow it in." They use both arguments against you when you try to get these items in. This is something the parliamentary secretary could do without too much disturbance to the bill or to Schedule A. So far as I am concerned it certainly would not change the revenue that the federal treasury gets.

Unless I am sadly mistaken about the purpose of item 42711-1, first of all, it is not in the way of a renumbering or a re-expressing of what is covered by 40924-1. It deals with a rather different matter. It is part of an attempt that the house is being asked to make to correct a ruling of the Tariff Board which deemed front-end loaders were to be covered under the same tariff item as tractors, and therefore let in duty free. This led to many representations, including some from the opposite side of the house, that this was detrimental to Canadian industry. For example, I think there was a plant in London, Ontario, which was making this equipment. The proposed item 40938-1 is designed to clarify this matter. Item 42711-1 is to make clear that if the tools in question are for the purpose of attachment to the type of tractors in question, but are not for farm purposes, then they are covered by the duty in question.
It is my understanding of the will of parliament, expressed in Schedule A of the Customs Tariff Act, that implements and machinery for farm purposes come in duty free, but that farm equipment is not included in this duty free provision under 40924-1 in quite the way the hon. member would like it to be. This may be something that requires further study and possibly further change, but I conclude by repeating that 40924-1 is not to be found in the bill that is before the committee of the whole in any way whatever.

Mr. Chairman, the position of the New Democratic party has been stated on the resolution stage and also on the second reading stage by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. Therefore my remarks will be very brief but pointed.
The first matter I would like to draw to the attention of the parliamentary secretary is that there were three points set forth in the
Customs Tariff
statement by the Consumers' Association of Canada when they presented their brief before the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs.
The first point refers to the desirability of stronger direct representation of consumers in future Canadian trade negotiations. I would assume that the reason for that was the shabby treatment that the different organizations and groups within Canada received prior to the entry by officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce into the Kennedy round negotiations. I think I should put on record that the trade unions were not contacted in any way whatever with regard to their position on the Kennedy round and, to say the least, the representation of the farmers was very slight. I understand they were contacted prior to the negotiations but certainly never during the negotiations. When one thinks of the great changes that took place concerning agricultural produce one hopes that in the future officials of the department will contact these different groups to get their views on these important matters.
The association's second point concerned the regional impact in Canada of relaxation of Canadian trade restrictions, and the third point concerned the importance of continuing efforts to reduce those impediments to international trade which will still remain after the Kennedy round tariff cuts are completed. I would hope the officials would take these points into greater consideration the next time they commence to negotiate with regard to tariff changes.
It would be fair to say that the role of Canada is to develop the principle of free trade and that the GATT agreement was one of the necessary steps to achieve this goal. Tariff protection has been a valuable instrument of nation building, and economic nationalism was necessary to political independence and the creation of a national economy. Now differences arise only with respect to the rate and the manner in which tariff changes should be established, whether they should be unilateral, bilateral or multilateral, or selectively by sector. As a result of the negotiations it appears that Canada, as with other countries, set the pace toward multilateral free trade; yet it has experimented in selective arrangements such as the automotive pact.

There has been a transfer from the dominance of tariff protection to an awareness of

the penetration of foreign ownership in Canada. It may be argued that tariff protection created Canadian industries but not Canadian firms, when one appreciates the expansive drive of United States corporations in the late nineteenth century and early twentieth century in developing Canadian industries but not Canadian firms. Instead of creating Canadian entrepreneurship capable of leading Canadian economic growth, the tariff approach has created a branch plant economy. The growth of foreign ownership in Canada has been phenomenal. When one realizes, according to the Watkins report, that in 1964 we had foreign ownership to the value of $27 billion in Canada and that now it probably has soared to around $35 billion, one can appreciate the immensity of the problem. When one appreciates the United States penetration of the Canadian economy and understands that 80 per cent of foreign ownership has been on the part of United States companies, one realizes this is a very important matter. When one appreciates that in the auto industry they have almost 100 per cent control, in the chemical industry 78 per cent control and in the rubber industry 77 per cent control, this underlines the importance of the problem at this time.
When I read the statement of the Prime Minister over the week end and his assessment of the just society to date as well as his almost total acknowledgement of treating our economy as an integrated economy with the United States I was very disappointed. When I hear the statements of cabinet ministers with regard to their continentalist views it makes me realize they have become aposto-lates of Canadian nationalism instead of apostles of Canadian nationalism. They have denounced and set aside Canada's number one nationalist, Walter Gordon. They have paid no attention to date to the Watkins report. They have failed to heed the serious warnings of the Toronto Star. I might say that the Toronto Star has taken a very active part in pointing out to Canadians the serious problem we have with regard to foreign ownership. In fact they have prepared a pamphlet which all Canadians should have setting forth the danger of the penetration that has been made in the economic sector of our economy. One fears that once they have controlled the economic sector the time is short with regard to any political independence.
It is very difficult to find at the present time one cabinet minister who is a Canadian nationalist. I have only found two Liberal

members, the hon. member for Scarborough and the hon. member for York North, who have definitely stated they are Canadian nationalists. I notice that the Minister of Defence Production has made an attempt to participate in this debate and therefore he may get up to say that he is a Canadian nationalist. However, I have not found one cabinet minister who has definitely stated he is a nationalist with regard to our economy. Having had no success with the cabinet ministers, I shall ask the parliamentary secretary just what his position is with regard to this very important problem. There are quite a few parliamentary secretaries. I notice two more in the house at the moment. Perhaps they could set forth their position with regard to Canadian economic nationalism because of the seriousness of the problem. I shall also ask the parliamentary secretary to speak a little more fully with regard to that multinational corporation, the auto industry. I fully appreciate that he comes from a riding that has within it automotive businesses. He appreciates the penetration of United States companies in this field.
Last night I mentioned that it seems to me to be a very sad and sorry situation that in Canada, which is in the position of developing from having a population of 20 million people to having a population of probably 35 million people at the end of the century, we must, as the Prime Minister said in his statement last night, let the automotive business go to our friends in the United States. When I think of countries like Sweden, which has a population of between 7 million and 8 million people, having a very thriving auto business it makes me rather sick to think that we have defaulted in this particular area and have undertaken no research and development to establish a separate automotive industry which could provide Canadians with a car that would suit Canadian conditions and climate and also build up our export trade. This is a very important factor. I am happy to see the Minister of Defence Production agrees with me. He probably will persuade his cabinet colleagues that this is an area in which we should become very active. When we consider that we will double our population by the year 2000 it would seem that this is a field in which we should start working right away.
I might mention the experience some of us had in respect of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs with regard to the Kennedy round and the chemical industry.

Representatives of that industry appeared before the committee and the problems that are being experienced by it were set forth. I might tell my colleagues in the house just what the problem in the chemical industry is. The chemical industry has developed to such a state that it has gone beyond the status of being nationalist. When an order is received for a chemical they now use a computer. Information is fed into the computer concerning the material, labour and transportation costs, and taxes. Out of the computer comes the answer concerning where the order should be placed. It indicates that in an economy like ours where there is a domination of foreign ownership in the chemical field no concern is given to the need for Canadian industry to put a drive on in the export market in the chemical field. This applies in many fields. This situation is causing many of us concern.
When we consider the immense corporations in the United States and the research and development programs they have, we realize that this leaves the branch plant economy of Canada in a very awkward and weak position with regard to a drive on exports. This is the situation in respect of developing our Canadian economy. The key to economic growth is the export market. When we have to depend on United States firms to do the research and development and when these United States firms are creating branch plants as branches which will serve the domestic market and not the export market, this is an indication of the weakened position we in Canada are in.
I might also relate to the parliamentary secretary an experience I had on a plane while coming to Ottawa. I met a man who is involved in the advertising business. He went to his bank to borrow money for expansion purposes. He said the amount required was modest. The bank refused him the money to expand his plant. Later he had a call from the bank manager. I notice that the parliamentary whip is very attentive because at one time he was a bank manager. What really happened was that the bank manager invited him back at a later date and asked him whether he would be interested in selling his plant to a group of Americans. The bank manager said that they were prepared to finance the group of Americans who were prepared to pay in the neighbourhood of $2 million for this Canadian company.
Here we have a case of a Canadian entrepreneur wishing to borrow a meagre amount
Customs Tariff
of money for plant expansion in his particular business who is refused by the bank and then later invited back by the bank manager who attempts to persuade him that he should sell his Canadian business to a United States group in which case the savings of the Canadian people would be used by the Canadian bank to finance the purchase.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
This mood and attitude have pervaded the minds not only of those who occupy the government benches but the minds of other people in Canada. We must do something about this now. It is all very well to talk about trade problems, but we must appreciate some of the practical problems which face Canadian businessmen today. These people need to be encouraged by the government to develop a Canadian economy controlled by Canadians. We need a research and development program supported and assisted by the government in order to increase Canadian exports to the point that we are not dependent on these branch plant operations of United States companies.
The statements by the parliamentary secretary and other hon. members in respect of non-tariff barriers are absolutely accurate. There are problems in respect of quotas and border taxes. The hon. member for Wellington outlined the problems caused by a two-price system in some countries. I was a little surprised that he drew attention to the central electrical authority in England which, according to officials of Canadian General Electric, refused a bid by Canadian General Electric in respect of heavy electrical equipment for use in England.
We hear representations and allegations during the committee stage of the Kennedy Round negotiations against Sweden. It was rather striking that during one meeting the vice president of Canadian General Electric cried about barriers established by England and Sweden, because in an address by the president of Canadian General Electric, which was included in a pamphlet distributed to members of the committee, he asked for special treatment by the Ontario hydro commission in respect of equipment they provided. That company was asking for the very thing it was complaining about other companies doing. This is a part of the problem we are experiencing. Canadian General Electric should put its own house in order not only in this field but in the field of pricing. We are aware of the difficulties this company has

encountered in respect of the fixing of prices in other countries.
We also have special treatment for Canadian manufacturers, and I am not talking about defence contracts or decrying them. All I am saying is that we do have these problems in our own jurisdiction and that they should be studied in depth by the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs in order that we can be sure that trade officials when they bargain with these people are well informed about the feelings and views of government members. I ask the parliamentary secretary, who is a very able gentleman, to make known his personal views in respect of these very important problems.

Mr. Chairman, I intended to make a few remarks at the resolution stage. However, being a co-operative fellow and having been asked by the parliamentary secretary to wait until today, I have done so. I should also like to direct attention to the fact that at the resolution stage comments were made by members of the opposition to the effect that the minister was not here. In view of the manner in which the parliamentary secretary has handled this whole shebang, and in view of the fact he seems to have knowledge of this department at his fingertips, I have the feeling that, much to the chagrin of the minister, the minister has not been missed. Let me compliment the parliamentary secretary for a wonderful job.
You are not bucking for a call, are you?

My comments will be restricted to those remarks about the Kennedy round negotiations which seem to indicate they are the cause of all our customs tariff problems. The parliamentary secretary mentioned that the advantage we obtained last year in our export position was due to the Kennedy round negotiations. I take some issue with that statement. They had a lot to do with it but, as he admitted, the automotive pact had a tremendous effect.
No Canadian wants to be a hewer of wood and drawer of water. We all want to see Canadian industry manufacture goods and export them. We want other nations to accept our manufactured goods tariff free or at low tariffs. The purpose of tariffs is to protect jobs. Customs tariffs account for about 15 per cent or 16 per cent of our national revenue, and I sometimes wonder whether we are still interested in the original idea of protecting

jobs or in gaining revenue. There is always a danger of such a shift in purpose.
This bill is partly the result of the Kennedy round negotiations. We have heard members on both sides of the house refer to problems in respect of the glove, shoe and salt industries. These people are constantly at the heels of officials who attempt to negotiate tariffs on a national basis. This is political activity. It seems to me that the Kennedy round negotiations were intended to ensure that eventually every country would produce those articles it could produce most efficiently. There will always be barriers because of physical situations. Exports and imports are restricted not only because of a desire to protect certain industries but to attain a financial balance. This plays a great part in the over-all picture.
The European economic market has been in existence for some time, and it was hoped that trade problems in that area would by this time have been solved. We all know they still have problems in France. Potato growers there do not agree with the negotiations carried out by their administrators. Other industries in the European common market find themselves in positions far short of their expectations so far as trade patterns are concerned. The original concept was that countries which could most efficiently produce certain products would produce those products. This has not been accomplished.
In long term trading plans we cannot rely to a great extent on the Kennedy round negotiations. We are not all angels and we have certain established interests. When we consider the automotive pact we must realize that it is a plan to create a balance of trade in this industry between Canada and the United States. It does not take into account the dollar balance. What we are saying is that we will accept automotive parts from the United States tariff free as long as the United States will accept an equivalent amount of trade. This is what I have been advocating for the last ten years. We must gear our export-import plans to a volume balance rather than a dollar balance.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Let me give an example. We export each year $28 million or $30 million in reserve gas. This means we have sold to the United States or others a reserve of billions of cubic feet of gas. It also means that we have imported $28 million or $30 million of manufactured goods, radios, and so on. As long as we have the
December 3, 1968

natural resources, electrical energy, aluminum, gas and oil, we can maintain our balance of trade and still be largely unemployed. So that is not the secret. The secret is a balance of trade in man-hours. In other words, we should say to the world: We will allow imports tariff free of so many manhours as long as we can export the equivalent amount.
That is what the automotive pact is. The strange thing is that although the automotive pact, as the parliamentary secretary said himself, has meant an increase since 1963 from $300 million to $4 billion, we seem hesitant to expand this policy. I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary or one of the ministers can say why we cannot include in the automotive agreement tractors, outboard motors and motorcycles. All these items take about the same amount of skill to manufacture and the industries pay about the same wages. Why cannot we expand the automotive pact still further to other industries?
Two years ago the minister of forestry cried out for another type of pact for the forest industry. Surely by expanding the automotive pact, initially engulfing those industries which are closely allied and then by arrangement allowing other industries to come under the same type of agreement, we would find ourselves on the road to a possible solution of this problem. We will not always enjoy a balance of trade. We will not always be able to export to other countries and solve our financial problems in this way.
GATT was mentioned, the general agreement on tariffs and trade. It is not commonly known that the members of this agreement spend a great deal of time trying to find loopholes in it. I wonder about the value of this agreement, when one considers that we have fantastic transportation problems from coast to coast. In Germany, for instance, what might be called a quasi-subsidization of the transportation business allows the barge system on the canals to be used so that industry anywhere in Germany is, for all practical purposes, right on the seacoast. There is practically no transportation cost involved. These are the things the members of this agreement worry about. The agreement is not working out as well as we thought it would.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to emphasize this point to the parliamentary secretary. He has already pointed out that we have an idea of what constitutes a very good agreement, namely, the automotive pact. Can we not expand this policy and use the same idea with other industries or relate other 29180-218

BONAVENTURE AND GASPi TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
Mr. Alexandre Cyr (for Mr. LeBlanc,
Rimouski) moved the second reading of Bill No. S-12, respecting the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company, Limited.
He said:

Mr. Speaker, this bill is not new. Indeed, the same bill under the No. S-33 was passed at the other place during the last session, after having been studied by the standing committee on transport and communications. After first reading in this house, as indicated in Votes and Proceedings for February 28 1968, it was placed on the order paper for second reading on February 28, 1968. However, that debate was not held because the houses were dissolved on April 23 last.
At this point, I should like to quote the explanatory note, of this bill:
The purpose of this hill is to resolve doubts as to whether the company may dispose of its undertaking to a company incorporated under or subject to the laws of any province of Canada.
The company was incorporated on April 12 1907. Under section 11 of chapter 64 of the statutes for 1906-07, that company was forbidden to merge. Under section 5 of the act respecting The Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company, Limited, namely chapter 86 of the statutes for 1955, the constitution of that company was amended. Indeed, under that act, disposal of the undertaking is allowed subject to the approval of the shareholders and that of the Canadian Transport Commission.
We feel that the act passed in 1955 does not clearly grant the company the power to sell or dispose of its assets to a company which does not fall within the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament. The company to which

DEBATES	December 3, 1968
The Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company, Limited wishes to sell its assets is the Quebec Telephone Company which was incorporated under a Quebec charter.
Mr. Speaker, doubts concerning the power to sell or dispose of its assets to a company which does not fall within the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament would be resolved if the following sentence were added to section 11 of the constitution:
Such sale or disposal, whether of the whole or any part of the said undertaking, rights and properties, may be so made by the company to any company or person, whether within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada or not, authorized to carry on a business included within the objects or powers of the company.
That alteration is very simple since its sole purpose is to grant in fact to the company the power to dispose of its assets in favour of the Quebec Telephone Company which holds a provincial charter.
For your information, Mr. Speaker, it is important to point out that since 1953 that company has been under the full control of the Quebec Telephone Company, since the latter holds approximately 99.9 per cent of the shares. The areas served by the latter company are all located in Quebec or close to it, and the managements of the two companies merged in 1952. Actually, the staff of the Quebec Telephone Company looks after the operations of the said company. In fact, there is some overlapping and needless expenditures.
It is very important, therefore, to recall that Quebec Telephone is acquiring the assets of the said company in order to avoid needless expenditures resulting from the partial overlapping of the services of the two companies.
We therefore ask hon. members to consider that bill kindly and to agree to its being considered in committee before third reading.

This type of development has been of recent date in the United States. At the turn of the century man looked upon himself as a great enterpriser. He went out and conquered a particular area of business. He staked it out for himself. He worked hard and managed to get other workers to work with him. He has to go on and on, like the man with the barns, who just kept on growing larger and larger crops, and who, when he asked, what he should do, received the answer, "Build bigger barns." speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill which will be based on this resolution will represent a major step forward in the evolution of the international monetary system. With the establishment of the scheme to create special drawing rights in the International Monetary Fund, for the first time nations will be able to create international monetary reserves, to meet the requirements of the whole system, by deliberate and joint action. The main objective of the bill will be to provide for Canada's participation in this exciting development.
The bill will set out a number of amendments to the articles of agreement of the
I.M.F. to provide for the operation of the scheme to create special drawing rights. It also will set out certain amendments modifying the rules and practices of the existing operations of the fund to reflect the experience of almost a quarter of a century.
The government hopes that this legislation will have the wholehearted support of this house and that its passage will not be

delayed. This should not, of course, exclude a thorough consideration of its various aspects in committee. The last time this house had an opportunity to consider these matters at some length was in March 1966 when a bill to increase Canada's quotas in the International Monetary Fund and the I.B.R.D. was before the house. At that time the late Colin Cameron and other members called for the creation of the equivalent in the international field of the managed currency which all modem countries use in their domestic economies. A good deal of interest was shown in the broader issues at that time, and the matter was discussed in the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, of which I was then the chairman.
As members who participated in that discussion well know, the resolution before us represents the culmination of more than four years of intensive study and negotiation by ministers and senior officials in the group of ten and by the executive directors of the
I.M.F. The essential soundness of the proposed scheme is a tribute to their efforts. The fact that such complex discussions were begun in time and successfully concluded is a reflection of the international co-operation in economic and financial affairs which we have come to expect in the post world war II period, but which had failed to develop significantly up to that time.
At the centre of this co-operation has been the I.M.F. The fund was conceived, along with the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, during and came into being immediately following the second world war. The results of narrowly nationalistic policies were evident everywhere and the memories of the disastrous consequences of the self-defeating economic policies of the 1930s were still fresh in people's minds. The fund's founding fathers therefore set out to create an international authority to establish and maintain a high standard of conduct in international monetary and economic affairs and which would be endowed with the facilities and the financial resources to help countries to live up to this standard. The significant success achieved by the I.M.F. since 1946 has contributed to the growth of world trade and payments and consequently to the prosperity which Canadians now enjoy. Canada is heavily dependant on international trade and the availability of capital for its prosperity. We have therefore a very large stake in the success of the I.M.F.
Consequently Canada made a noteworthy contribution to the negotiations at Bretton
December 3, 1968

Finance
competent and experienced forum. Membership in the scheme will be open to all members of the fund. SDR's will be traded among monetary authorities for convertible currencies. They will not be usable for direct intervention in the foreign exchange markets or for other private transactions. SDR's will be assets owned by a participating country and recorded on the books of the special drawing account in the International Monetary Fund. They will be freely and unconditionally available with two exceptions:
(i)	They will only be usable for balance of payments needs, not solely to change the composition of a country's reserves;
(ii)	A country making an average net use over five years of more than 70 per cent of its net cumulative allocation of SDR's will incur a reconstitution, in other words a repurchase, obligation. These rules are to help ensure that the new asset will not be abused in its use and will be held by all the participating countries.
The new asset is a fiduciary asset, that is, its value is based on the willingness of countries to accept it in exchange for convertible currencies. It is not backed by any particular asset and in that respect is like the domestic currencies of most countries. Decisions to create SDR's will be taken by the board of governors of the International Monetary Fund on the basis of a proposal by the managing director which has been concurred in by the executive directors. A majority of 85 per cent of the voting power of the participants will be required.
SDR's will be created to meet the long run growth in global demand for reserves-not to meet the balance of payments needs of individual countries. Consequently the decision to create them will be taken every five years and the amount decided will be distributed in equal proportions annually. Of course, if circumstances alter considerably during the five year period it will be possible to make appropriate adjustments in the annual distributions.
SDR's will be used to obtain convertible currencies from other participants either directly or through the special drawing account acting as intermediary. Normally currencies will be acquired from participants with a strong balance of payments and reserve position. A participant's obligation to accept SDR's ceases when its holdings are three times the net cumulative amount of SDR's allocated to it. They will be gold value

guaranteed, that is, their value will be protected against changes in the value of national currencies, and they will earn a moderate rate of interest-1J per cent-the cost of which will be assessed against members in proportion to the net cumulative allocation of SDR's to them.
Newly created SDR's will be distributed to participants in the same proportion as their quotas in the International Monetary Fund. Consequently, if it were decided to create $1 billion of the new asset, Canada would receive $35 million of SDR's. No offsetting liability will back this new creation other than the obligation to accept, in certain circumstances, the asset from others for convertible currencies.
A number of other amendments to the articles of agreement of the International Monetary Fund will be proposed in the bill to modify the rules and practices of the existing machinery of the Fund. Most of these proposals are rather technical and represent no more than a clarification or codification of practices developed over the years and followed currently by the Fund. Others take into account the existence in reserves of SDR's and the operation of the special drawing account. I shall mention here only the most important of the proposed amendments.
Henceforth a general increase in quotas in the International Monetary Fund will require an 85 per cent majority vote of the governors instead of 80 per cent. This will bring the practice in the fund in line with that proposed for SDR's. Requests for purchases of a country's gold tranche, which corresponds to the 25 per cent of its subscription paid in gold or U.S. dollars, are now created automatically on a de facto basis. One of the amendments will make the use of the Fund's resources in the gold tranche legally automatic. Another amendment will remove the present limitation on making gold tranche purchases for meeting capital transfers. A member will be able to make gold tranche purchases even though they are to meet what might be regarded as a large or sustained outflow of capital.
A transaction charge of one half of 1 per cent is currently levied on gold tranche drawings, and this will be removed. Henceforth remuneration at the rate of 1J per cent per annum will be payable on creditor positions in the fund. In most years since 1963 Canada has been in a substantial creditor position. There are other amendments which are less important and I will be happy to
December 3, 1968

discuss any or all of them at later stages of debate if it is the wish of the house.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the bill will propose a change in the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act which will permit special drawing rights to be held in and counted as part of Canada's exchange fund. In this way we will have authority to fulfil the undertaking in the new scheme to accept and hold the new special drawing rights. The government hopes that it shall, in the near future, be able to notify the managing director of the Fund that the Canadian parliament has passed the necessary measures to enable Canada to participate in this historic step forward.

Mr. Chairman, the rather hurried and capsuled description of the proposed legislation-and I do not wish to criticize the parliamentary secretary when I say this-is something which, in my view, confirms the requirement that, following the passage of this legislation and the printing of the bill, the government should immediately place a resolution on the order paper-and I am quite prepared on behalf of the opposition to accept a motion from the appropriate minister without further notice- that the bill shall be referred to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs for examination and, if necessary, for the purpose of hearing certain representations. I think that, while some people may perhaps criticize the desire to examine this legislation in greater detail and to hear representations in connection with it, as being an unnecessary step, what we have experienced in the last 18 months is a clear indication that the methods used by the countries to exchange their currencies and to maintain the stability of their currencies, and in fact all the operations of the I.M.F., have come under the most extreme strain.
There have been crises with respect to the two reserve currencies, twice with regard to the pound, the last being in November of 1967, and a massive assault on the dollar in February and March of this year. The last one was a few weeks ago with regard to the franc. The unfortunate part is that the rhythm of this cycle of financial crises is accelerating. It is almost as though we were watching a boat starting to rock while at the same time we possessed a greater force which accentuated that rocking. Soon the rhythm will accelerate and the effects on the boat will become more pronounced. It will be that
Finance
when we go over the brink it will be too late,
and therefore I think it is of the greatest importance that we as Canadians contribute to the desirable stability in international monetary relationships.
All types of governments participate in these relationships, and I do not think there is any country, whether it be socialistic or capitalistic, that has a monopoly in or an exclusive recipe for the maintenance of prosperous conditions in that country. Why must there be additional international credits? Simply because the U.S. dollar and the pound sterling which have been used by the International Monetary Fund as reserve monetary units have come under increasing internal strains, and this has been the weakness of the International Monetary Fund in recent years. The U.S. dollar is affected of course in its value by actions on the domestic scene, and all too often those efforts which are made domestically in the United States in connection with problems of inflation or of stimulation of the economy have opposite or complicated effects when it comes to the international market.
We have seen that the strain on the U.S. dollar came about this last spring as a result of the continuing pattern of deficiency on the balance of payments accounts while the United States was active in its trade pattern, its foreign aid, the war in Viet Nam and in a number of other fields. The net result was that known holdings of U.S. dollars by Foreign interests last March exceeded by about $4,000 million the U.S. gold holdings. The reason why the pound sterling has been under severe attack is similar. That currency too has become a unit of international holdings, particularly by countries, banks and individuals in the Middle and the Far East. It is a currency of international commerce. The Lord only knows, the British have been having problems at home, many of them of their own making, and yet the pound, which is suffering such vicissitudes on the domestic scene, is supposed to be the unit of stability on the international scene. We have seen now that this cannot continue.
So far as Canada is concerned, those of us who were here last February and March were well aware of how close we came to the point of having to devalue our currency. The then minister of national revenue was indiscreet in indicating a figure on television, when in actual fact the correct figure was somewhat lower. The then minister of finance had to rebuke his colleague for being indiscreet on

television, but for the administration of the day it was par for the course. To me it was just a measure of irresponsibility.
As a matter of fact, just what was the pressure on the currencies? As we know, there was a flight from the franc to the German mark, and there was a tremendous amount of speculation with regard to the mark because it was anticipated there would be a revaluation upward. There are movements of floating capital, which is known as hot money, which are undertaken to improve the value of the capital as a result of fractional changes in valuation.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
When it was decided by the French government that the franc would not be devalued, and that the Germans were not going to revalue the mark upwards, about which the Germans were not too enthusiastic, in one day there was an immediate flight of $300 million from the German mark to United States dollars. So you observe, Mr. Chairman, this movement back and forth.
If the United States dollar is affected by this crisis, then so is the Canadian dollar. Although we might be standing by relatively innocently on the side, as a very interested bystander in a currency crisis for one of our trading partners in western Europe, we are caught up by the splash. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we in Canada have a special interest in the liquidity of the international reserve units, particularly unit that is being set up under these proposals for special drawing rights which are available in times of crisis.
I indicated, Mr. Chairman, that we are going to get caught up by the splash. May I point out that since 1963 Canada has become even more involved. I wish that Canada were not so involved with the U.S. dollar, that there were more options open to Canada in dealing with domestic situations and also with our own position in the international market. We have what the Minister of Finance, I think for reasons of semantics, wishes to call a target; but what I call a ceiling, call it what you will, Mr. Chairman, Canada may hold between $2.55 billion and $2.6 billion worth of United States obligations.
What has happened since this crisis last March, Mr. Chairman? First of all, we are down to holdings of $2.55 billion. Of that sum, $500 million consists of non-negotiable United States securities which Canada retained as a result of realizing some of its

convertible United States obligations. This Canada had to do as the price of relief from the mandatory guide lines that were set last January, and the manner in which we were involved during the currency crisis last spring. This situation is severely limiting Canada's options for dealing with its financial problems at home and on the international market.
I was glad to hear from the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman, that talks are now going on with the United States treasury officials on this particular subject. Less than one year ago, Mr. Chairman, I was told there was no problem with the ceiling. I do not take credit for my remarks, but pressures here and there, have had some effect on finance department officials. I am not alone in my views. Nevertheless it is conceivable that some of the remarks made by Canadian delegates-chiefly myself-during the Canadian-United States interparliamentary union meeting in March may be bearing fruit. I believe that this so-called ceiling, if we must have one, and I say we should not, should be raised; it should be increased by at least $1 billion.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this ceiling is having a deleterious effect on our domestic financial operations in that, our trading pattern having been what it has during the last 18 months, the Bank of Canada has found itself under obligation to enter the exchange market to pick up U.S. dollars. To do so it has put into circulation millions of Canadian dollars. In other words, it has had to skim off the market of U.S. dollars within Canada to keep us under the ceiling.
We know that last week, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance engaged in some refinancing operations and was able to prepay some obligations falling due in 1969. At the present time he has been able to pick up a little spare cash. As a matter of fact, he indicated that he would not have to go to the capital market again shortly.
That may be his plan, Mr. Chairman, but frankly I can see a danger arising which may make the minister go to the market. The minister will need cash to go to the exchange market to buy up U.S. dollars, because we are pushing through the ceiling that has been imposed upon us. If our holdings go up, or threaten to go up, to $2.7 billion, $2.75 billion or $2.8 billion, the minister has to skim off the extra up to $200 in United States funds, and for this he will have to go to the market.

What will be the result then, Mr. Chairman? There will be an upward pressure on our domestic interest rates. This will bring in U.S. money for investment purposes, and away we go again as the wheel turns. The system is self-perpetuating and certainly of no assistance to the government in maintaining an even hand on the tiller, so far as our financial situation is concerned. It is for that reason among others that the sooner we get out of this strait-jacket the better.
At the present time, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian government's credit position is lamentable. The bond market is in disarray. If hon. members want to read something that is truthful, that has no political bias or partisan approach-something which some might try to ascribe to my remarks-then let them read the remarks of the president of the Bank of Montreal yesterday. They are a clear indication of what is thought of the bond market. Let hon. gentlemen opposite consult with their financier friends-and the Liberal party does have friends in Toronto around Bay street, or do they now?-and get a frank answer from those who are in the bond business or the banking field about the position of Canadian bonds.
We know how the level of interest rates has had a general effect on housing, Mr. Chairman. To assist in the correction of this problem the government must start at square one. We must first attack this artificial ceiling that we have on U.S. exchange holdings. Then we shall see that we can have greater freedom to act on behalf of Canadians.

The parliamentary secretary gave us a brief outline in capsule form of many of the main features of the bill-the special drawing rights, that these were new and were not replacing other reserve units, and so on and so forth. I do not think I need to comment on all those things. I can only say that we will appreciate being able to get hold of the bill. I trust this resolution will pass this evening. Finally I should like to know from the parliamentary secretary whether there is an undertaking from the government that the bill will be referred to the finance committee for study in the new year.
