speechtext:
Although I do not wish to detract from the parliamentary secretary's sense of history in bringing forward this proposal, I think it is necessary to express a note of caution, so that we may deal with this proposal in as realistic a fashion as possible.
The proposal before us was developed after a great deal of work and negotiation, yet it is but one step on the difficult road we must thread in finding a monetary system that will work satisfactorily. In this respect it is worth noting that the special drawing rights referred to by the parliamentary secretary, which will be dealt with in the bill, do not help with respect to the current problem that has been facing monetary authorities the world over in recent weeks. The Financial Post of November 23 has this to say on the matter:
Contrary to some views, the present money crisis is not the type of problem the proposed Special Drawing Rights (SDRs)-or international reserve currency to supplement gold, US$ and sterling- was designed to correct. "SDRs are designed to improve world-wide liquidity, not to stabilize an imbalance between one country and another," a senior Ottawa official said. "It would be wrong to use SDRs-if they were in operation-in a situation like the present French-German problem," he said.
The parliamentary secretary also noted that in the proposal before us, which is to establish special drawing rights, there is no provision to replace gold or other reserves. That, itself, indicates the role this measure will have in dealing with our monetary problems.
I submit that we can consider this resolution in a realistic way only if we consider recent developments in world monetary affairs. No doubt hon. members are aware of the events of the past few weeks. These were summed up neatly in the Globe and Mail of November 21, in an article reprinted from the New York Times and the Associated Press:
The latest international money crisis-the third in 12 months-has exposed once again what many regard as the Achilles heel of the otherwise successful international monetary system that was agreed upon by the leading nations almost 25 years ago.
But while the vulnerability of the system to crisis is now widely recognized, there is only the barest

December 3, 1968
Finance
beginning of official exploration of the most plausible remedy. The remedy is already seen to present numerous problems.
The Achilles heel is that the monetary system provides for fixed, steady exchange rates among currencies for trade and other international transactions, without any parallel binding obligation for nations to pursue policies that keep their international payments in balance at the exchange rate they have chosen.
Thus, in the view of thoughtful critics, the system makes it almost inevitable that from time to time one or another leading country "gets out of whack" with the others-yesterday Britain, today France and Germany, tomorrow, perhaps, the United States. For one reason or another, a nation's balance of payments drifts into chronic deficit or chronic surplus.
The article then points out the reasons for the difficulties that are encountered in the present system. I continue quoting:
The system provides a way out-devaluation of the exchange rate for a country in deficit, or revaluation for a country in surplus. But this is invariably a painful move for domestic political reasons. In the case of devaluation, for example, consumers pay more for imported goods and vacations abroad cost more. In the case of revaluation the profits of the important export industries are reduced and the farm sector may be badly hit.
The inadequacy of our present monetary system has been illustrated in the past few weeks by the panics that have developed when problems have arisen. There are special meetings of finance ministers and top monetary authorities of the countries involved. They patch up the difficulty that has been presented, and we go to another crisis a few months later.
Basically we lack enough liquidity money to cope with the amount of world trade as it has been expanding over the past decade. Canada, I think, is in a most vulnerable position, a position set out in the Financial Post of November 23, where the following words appear:
The stability of the C$, and that of many other currencies, could be upset if Europe's money troubles are not solved soon. But for the moment, France's problem is localized and Canadian observers are hopeful a solution can be found before trouble spreads.
It will take more than mere hope, Mr. Chairman, to solve our present problems. I ask, what action has Canada taken? Certainly, we have participated in some international negotiations. All the same, has there been any real Canadian initiative to deal with the problems at present facing us?
I wish to remind the committee of something the hon. member for York South, my parliamentary leader, said a week ago when

the Minister of Finance made a statement to the house about the recent situation I have just discussed. The hon. member for York South deplored the state of affairs that permits our monetary affairs to be so profoundly influenced by speculators, and people manipulating our international financial affairs. In this connection I was interested to read an article in the Ottawa Citizen of November 16 about these gnomes. The heading is, "Who and where are the gnomes?", and the article says this:
International currency crises are commonly blamed on the manipulations of the money market speculators, the gnomes of Zurich, or Wall Street, or even Bay street.
But it is not generally known just who these men are and how they practise their financial wizardry.
Money market experts paint this composite picture of the average gnome:
He is either the treasurer of a big corporation, or its adviser. His job is to advise his company, among other things, on the prospects for fluctuations in the value of the major currencies.
On his advice, his company will flit from currency to currency, trading the weak for the strong. In the process, it can both make money and guarantee protection for its assets.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Later the article goes on to discuss the influence which these speculators and "gnomes" have on the international monetary situation. The writer states:
Opinions on currency speculators vary. Government officials cite dangers in putting the interests of the company before country.
They point out speculation is self-generating. When dollars are sold in large volume, the exchange rate goes down triggering more sales. A heavy flight of dollars from the economy drains foreign exchange reserves which have to be shored up by the central bank.
Later the article says:
The decisions are not always easy. Sometimes a warning flashed by a currency adviser can have drastic implications for an economy.
Some observers have suggested that changes ought to be made in the present international monetary system. This question was discussed in the Globe and Mail of November 29:
The frequent recurrences of these monetary pressures raises a question as to whether the rigidities of the present fixed-exchange rates should be scrapped in favour of a more flexible system that permits a currency to fluctuate more than the present 1 per cent above or below its declared value.
There is an even broader framework to be considered, and it includes the proposal for the demonetization of gold entirely. This is dealt with in some detail by Mr. Harry
December 3, 1968

Johnson of the London School of Economics in an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail shortly after the gold crisis of last March. Mr. Johnson states:
Painful as the process may be, the attempt to preserve a special monetary role for gold may quickly end in the realization that the effort itself automatically demonetizes gold and converts the world monetary system into one based purely on bookkeeping transactions.
The hope must be that the world's monetary authorities can meanwhile keep their nerve. If they weaken, progress toward a rational international system will be put back a generation. The gold crisis which erupted again two weeks ago, forcing the emergency meeting in Washington, has long been anticipated by international monetary experts.
The only question has been when, and that question has now been answered. At the root of the crisis is the inherent logic of the gold exchange standard itself-the system under which the major countries maintain fixed exchange rates between their currencies by pegging them to convertibility into gold at a fixed price. As a means of providing an international monetary framework, however, this system is inherently illogical. For there is nothing in the laws of nature to guarantee that additional supplies of monetary gold will be forthcoming at precisely the rate required to provide for the world's growing needs for international money.
Instead, the world's supply of new monetary gold is dependant on the vagaries of:
-New discoveries and changing technologies of gold extraction;
-The demand of hoarders and commercial users;
-In the past 10 years, communist sales of gold from stockpiles or new production.
The article goes on to state:
It is true, theoretically, at least, that the gold standard has a self-stabilizing tendency. This is what Jacques Rueff, a leading French economist, is fond of arguing. If prices rise, gold production becomes less profitable, exerting a deflationary influence on the supply of monetary gold and hence on money. Conversely, falling prices stimulate new growth production, exerting an inflammatory influence on the supply of money and prices.
But these influences are slow and uncertain and are swamped by the forces of change in gold technology on the one hand and financial innovation on the other. In addition, government policy makers are not now prepared to abide the slow-grinding discipline of the gold standard.
Throughout the twentieth century the long-run inclination has been for new monetary gold supplies to increase less rapidly than the demand for international reserves. This tendency has been reinforced by government policies that have produced a secular inflation of prices. The result has been a growing scarcity of gold, which has been avertable in the short run by the substitution of national securities convertible into gold for gold itself, at the long-run cost, though, of rendering its system increasingly vulnerable to crises of confidence.
The article goes on to state:
Since the second world war the dollar has come to play the role previously played by sterling and
Finance
the system has arrived at precisely the same sort of crisis of confidence. Under the system a crisis of confidence is ultimately inevitable. But when and where it strikes depends on the appropriateness of the fixed exchange rates between the various national currencies mediated by the use of gold as an international monetary base.
Mr. Johnson concludes his study by stating:
A coldly rational view of the present international monetary situation would be (1) that gold is a very poor and unrealiable base for an international monetary system and (2) that as soon as possible it should be dispensed with. This implies (3) that gold held as a monetary reserve should be sold as rapidly as possible to anyone who has a non-monetary-and especially a misinformed-speculative use for it and (4) that international reserve money should instead be provided by an international credit operation.
This is, in fact, the way in which world central bank opinion has been moving. In particular, the plan for special drawing rights approved by the International Monetary Fund in Rio de Janiero last September implied the eventual replacement of gold by as pure a pure credit money as could be devised.
Some of these proposals have been dealt with by other observers who share the concern felt for the stability of the present monetary system. Mr. Alan Day of the London Observer service recently stated in an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of November 26:
Last week's financial crisis was a direct consequence of the unnecessary rigidity of the international monetary system. So long as each country regards any significant change in its exchange rate-either upward or downward-as a national defeat in the last ditch, the international system will continue to operate under quite unnecessary strain.
Later, Mr. Day writes:
Such is the rigidity of the international monetary system that the necessary adjustments can take place only after attempts to shore up a crumbling structure of exchange rates have been accompanied by speculation and rumours which put a heavy strain on currencies such as sterling and the dollar, whose true role in the situation is neutral.
The article goes on to suggest:
One approach which deserves the careful consideration of governments and bankers is the so-called "crawling peg". Each government would agree not to alter its exchange rate more than, say, 4 per cent in any one year. This would allow quite big adjustments to be made within fairly short periods of time, and, if used sensibly, could prevent the development of major imbalances. At the same time it would mean much smaller opportunities for speculators than the present adjustable peg system and would not create major uncertainties for businessmen who could, in any case, cover on the forward market.
The most important thing, however, is for governments and central banks to accept that the present system is too rigid with the consequence that when adjustments become unavoidable the strains are unnecessarily large.

December 3, 1968
Finance
It should be recognized that any change from a fixed exchange rate to a floating exchange rate does involve other considerations; there will be occasions when unusual strain is placed on the monetary system at which time complementary steps would be required such as selective exchange controls. A further question to be considered is the concentration of a large degree of economic and financial power in the hands of corporations whose head offices are in the United States. This is a consequence of the branch plant economy with which we have to contend to such a large extent today. The fact is that corporate decisions which bear no relation to the national interest could in many cases help produce a crisis situation. The step before us at this time is but one small step upon a long and difficult road. What is required from the Canadian government is more leadership and better leadership in finding a long term solution to monetary difficulties.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, the resolution now before the house reminds me singularly of the attitude of the Social Crediters who sat in this house some 22, 23 or 24 years ago, at the time of the first Bretton Woods agreements. At that time, the member for Lethbridge, Mr. Blackmore, warned the Canadian parliament of the consequences of the Bretton Woods agreements; today, we have come to exactly those consequences and results which were forecast 24 years ago by the Social Crediters who sat in roughly the same corner of the house.
At that time, Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King and the members of the cabinet found the remarks of the Social Crediters slightly crazy, slightly stupid; but let us look at the present world monetary crisis. Do not all the countries look like a group of stupid people trapped in a system of figures with which they cannot agree, which they cannot assimilate or accept, according to the physical possibilities they have to develop or make exchanges between each other?
We are now at grips with the same system; yet, 24 years ago the Social Crediters forecast the consequences of the situation in which we now find ourselves. At that time, the Social Crediters were laughed at, where they spoke of the fiasco that was awaiting the nations of the world that signed the Bretton Woods agreements.

Four days ago, one could read the following in Le Soleil of November 27, and I quote:
The future of money remains troubled.
Message from the French, from General de Gaulle, to the effect that the financial system is faulty. Will we need an international monetary reform? The heart is lacking to effect a national monetary reform; yet, the point has been reached where the necessity for international monetary reform is recognized.
Mr. Chairman, thanks to the opportunity afforded me by the study of the resolution introduced by the honourable Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), I am pleased, on behalf of Ralliement Creditiste, to let the house know what we think of this new arrangement within the International Monetary Fund.
With a view to creating new reserve assets to supplement gold-24 years ago it was gold, nothing other than gold which was to serve as the basis for international finance or the International Monetary Fund. On a national level, we have already known the famous gold standard as a guarantee for Canadian bank bills-whether it be bills issued by chartered banks, at that time; or since, by the Bank of Canada-and we thought gold was absolutely needed to give value to our Canadian dollar.
On May 1, 1940, to pay for our war effort, to equip our young Canadians and send them to the international slaughter, the Canadian dollar was taken off the gold standard, it was no longer backed by gold. There was not enough gold for the credit we needed to increase our participation in the world war. The gold reserve backing the Canadian dollar was abolished.
Mr. Chairman, new reserve assets are now being asked for the International Monetary Fund to supplement the gold reserve because there is no longer enough gold available. Some countries have no gold, others are supposed to have too much and others still have enough.
Let us take the example of France which objects to gold no longer being used to back money because it is said France has huge quantities of gold. Last year, less than twelve months ago, when the pound sterling was devaluated, when the British government was forced to impose tremendous restrictions on its people, our international and national financiers were praising France by saying that it had a sound monetary system; that it could no longer be crushed, and that the
December 3, 1968

Finance
French franc had a value which could not be affected.
Now France is facing the same problems as England less than a year ago, and they are now talking about reserve assets that would supplement gold in the international field. In fact, the resolution says:
-reserve assets that would supplement gold and reserve currencies in the participating countries foreign exchange reserves and would effect certain administrative and operational changes in the existing structure of the fund; and to permit the Exchange Fund Account to receive, hold and sell the new reserve assets.
As was said earlier by the hon. member who spoke before me, in order to supplement gold, we are now going to accept figures, credit, simple figures-scrip money as we call it-and we shall accept it as reserve currency in the I.M.F.
Twenty-five years ago, the Social Creditors were lunatics; today, there are other kinds of lunatics who are more dangerous than the Creditistes, because we advocate only one solution while the present system offers none.
They try this and that, but let us look at the editorials in the newspapers, one after the other. Nobody, not even the economists, are able to find a solution to the present international financial problem. They still poke fun at Social Credit which wants to use figures- according to the physical capabilities of a country to develop itself or to develop the whole world-which are equivalent to the work accomplished by peoples or by the Canadian people as far as Canada is concerned. Of course, these solutions are considered oversimple, they cannot be understood. I should say rather that they are understood but that one is paid not to understand them.

speechtext:
First, Mr. Chairman, I want to point out that this resolution results from decisions made during the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund held in Rio de Janeiro, in September 1967, in which participated the former minister of finance (Mr. Sharp).
On that occasion, Mr. Pierre-Paul Schweitzer, director of the International Monetary Fund stated that the arrangements considered at the meeting with regard to international liquid assets were the most imporant development since the Bretton Woods agreements in the field of international financial cooperation.
Since we are dealing with the Bretton Woods agreements and with a subsequent development, the special drawing rights, I want to recall the approach of the Ralliement Creditiste on this subject.
In 1945, during the discussion on the Bretton Woods agreements, as I said earlier, the Social Credit member for Lethbridge, who was an expert on financial matters, was considered tiresome because he spoke about money and monetary reform. He challenged parliament to prove him wrong but no member on the government side of the house took up the challenge.
The Social Credit proposals of the hon. member for Lethbridge were thought very tiresome. Nevertheless, he had cast a doubt on the ability of the International Monetary Fund and other instruments created by the Bretton Woods agreements to allow the debtor nations to pay their debts, since nothing compelled the creditor countries to accept the exports of the debtor countries.
Events in the world during the past 20 years have shown that the Bretton Woods agreements have not stopped practically all the member countries from devaluating their currency, as Canada did in 1963, when the Conservative government fell. Everybody remembers that. As we know, that devaluation came after a too marked imbalance in our commercial trade with the United States. At that time, Canada had to impose restrictions on the Canadian people in order to check the purchase of United States products.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
That measure simply confirmed what the hon. member for Acadia, Mr. Quelch, predicted, as is recorded on page 3134 of Hansard for December 6, 1945, and I quote:
That is to say-
He was talking about the proposals regarding the International Monetary Fund-
-if the United States consistently refuses to accept imports in exchange for its exports, thereby depriving other nations of dollars to pay for imports, then the fund can borrow or buy with gold, dollars from the United States to enable the debtor nations to balance their payments. But, mark you, it would be done by going into debt instead of by balancing trade and having an exchange of goods.
As the Bretton Woods agreements did not yet exist, money was borrowed from the United States. To-day, we can get into debt

December 3, 1968
Finance
by borrowing from the International Monetary Fund, by using special drawing rights, as we did during the 1963 monetary crisis.
Thus we can say that the Bretton Woods agreements did not prevent Canada from devaluating its money and getting into debt by borrowing from international organizations. So much so that we never slowed down this trend and to-day, our national debt amounts to $26 billion against the $18 or $19 billion at that time.
Mr. Chairman, those agreements did not solve the basic problems of Canada. The international control of money, as provided for in the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and the bill now under consideration, does not help Canada to distribute to its people our available products and services. It would be wiser to settle our own affairs and seek a solution to the problems of Canada.
On the contrary, the philosophy of the Bretton Woods agreements and any measure deriving therefrom, such as the bill now under consideration, prevent us from making possible all that would be humanly possible and advisable in our country, because we are entrusting the control of our credit and our money to other countries and foreign authorities, instead of keeping it here in parliament. The Bretton Woods agreements have been in force for 20 years, Mr. Chairman, and nothing has changed. The economic situation has worsened in Canada as elsewhere.
I get letters from Montreal where there are now 80,000 unemployed. What can the Bretton Woods agreements do to settle that problem? But they are given so much importance. It was nice-in fact, it was a magnificent spectacle-to see the other day in Paris or in Bonn, Germany, the representatives of the ten richest countries in the world decide whether or not France should devalue the franc. They were going to settle the future course of the monetary situation in France, and everyone expected a devaluation of the franc. The speculators were dealing on the stock exchange to make a profit and when General de Gaulle announced that the franc would not be devalued, some people pulled a long face.
Mr. Chairman, the French people have not been saved for all that. General de Gaulle declares that he will not devalue the franc, but he imposes tremendous restrictions on the French people, so that it is tantamount to a devaluation of the franc for the French consumer or purchaser.

Mr. Chairman, the same thing happened in Canada as well as in England. And today, they believe that with new agreements, or by supplementing the gold reserve deposited with the International Bank or the International Monetary Fund, they will improve the situation. The Bretton Woods agreements have done nothing for the last 24 years.
Mr. Chairman, nothing has changed. Let us listen to what the Minister of Finance said at the conference held in Rio de Janeiro on September 27, 1967-less than a year ago-and I quote:
The total volume of reserve assets held by monetary authorities in different countries depends at the present time essentially upon the gold production-
That is the Minister of Finance talking.
-to be used to improve the reserve position and the balance of payments of some of the principal countries as well as to serve their reserve policy. We are becoming increasingly aware of the inadequacy of that system.
These past few years, we have resorted to various devices which have allowed the system of sudden crises to continue.
What is the new solution proposed? The creation of special drawing rights, which are actually credits created out of nothing, which will only plunge us into debt, which we will have to reimburse and on which we will have to pay interest.
If a resolution can be introduced in parliament to allow us to have special drawing rights on the International Monetary Fund, how is it that the Canadian parliament, the parliament that is answerable to the people of Canada, cannot pass similar laws to enable the Canadian government to have special drawing rights on the Bank of Canada, in order to get the Canadian economy going?
Mr. Chairman, special drawing rights are needed in the case of the International Monetary Fund; but it seems impossible to create the same drawing rights on our own financial monetary institution, the Bank of Canada. The Liberals find that logical. Not one of them will speak against the Bretton Woods agreements. On the contrary, its benefit will be praised. And that is what is being presented to us as a new solution: the creation of special drawing rights which, in fact, are credits created out of nothing, out of paper gold, as General de Gaulle put it.
December 3, 1968

Here is what the French Minister of Finance, Mr. Michel Debre, had to say at the conference in Rio de Janeiro, and I quote:
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
It is often said that both problems would be solved by creating ex nihilo new monetary liquidities and by bringing those liquidities to the level of a new currency independent from gold and replacing gold. Is it really serious? It is impossible to create a currency out of nothing just as it is impossible to create political institutions out of nothing.
Mr. Chairman, in our opinion, money is created according to the real wealth which exists in a country like ours.
At the present time, as I said earlier, gold is no longer used as the standard for money in Canada. It is still used in the field of international relations because some countries still believe in gold, but it is a myth. Gold is used and people believe that the precious metal is the real basis for wealth, whereas in itself it constitutes only short lived wealth. If we wished to use gold, Mr. Chairman, to provide our families with food, lodging and clothing, that would be quite peculiar. We do not need gold, but clothing and food. We realize that more and more when we lay aside the question of gold to deal with that of credit based on the actual resources of a country. That is what the Ralliement Creditiste has been asserting for a long time.
Mr. Chairman, in the issue of Le Soleil which I quoted earlier, we can read the following:
The future of money remains gloomy. Even if the special drawing rights are freely accepted by all countries as part of their international monetary reserves-and nothing is so far from being sure-these rights would only enable nations to postpone a little consideration of problems which cause inflation.
That means that nothing is solved yet.
And I continue the quotation:
The newspaper adds this: "The recent experience has once again demonstrated that an attitude of levity towards currency is not even a good policy in the end-When this lesson has been learned, perhaps a monetary conference will serve some purpose. For instance, can the nations who want a certain amount of freedom towards world monetary discipline find a respectable way of ensuring it; they can be a little more flexible in their exchange rates".
The paper concludes: "Rigid exchange rates and rigid inflationary financing demonstrated that this is a fine recipe to produce chaos".
And there are bumps to go with that.
Finance
In La Presse of November 20, this is what Cyrille Felteau had to say. I quote:
Lessons from a monetary crisis.
In the eye of the layman and the experts, the new and serious difficulties the franc is going through prove beyond all doubts that the international monetary system is sick. In any event, that is what General de Gaulle and Mr. Couve de Murville have been saying for quite some time. In his televised speech to the nation, the French premier did not fail to emphasize this important point.
Those who participate in the system will have to take stock of themselves, if they want to prevent other jolts of this kind, which could degenerate into an economic depression on an international scale.

I also thank my colleagues for allowing me to continue my remarks. However, I shall not take unfair advantage of the opportunity given to me. This shows the advantages of the democratic system which allows one to express one's views even if they are different from those of others.
Mr. Chairman, I continue to quote from Mr. Felteau's article:
The participants in the system will have to take hold of themselves if they want to avoid other crises of this sort which can lead to an international economic depression.
I should be noted that the present crisis opposing the franc to the German mark is the third crisis to shake the world monetary system in twelve months.
There have been three international monetary crises in. the space of twelve months.
In November 1967, the pound sterling fell. In March 1968, there was a rush on gold-
There was a general rush on gold.
-followed, in the spring, by a running away from the franc and the pound sterling.
In 1968, nobody wanted francs or pounds sterling.
Many Canadians will also remember that in January of that year, the Canadian dollar was saved in extremis.
It was almost a case of administering the last rites.
All this shows that most currencies, with the exception of the American dollar, are more or less vulnerable.

December 3, 1968
Finance
And even the American dollar gave rise to speculations last spring.
In spite of several important differences, the present situation in France is similar to that which has existed in Great Britain for years.
As I was saying earlier Mr. Chairman, was France, a year ago, not considered as the country with the strongest monetary system in the world? And one year later, France is driven into a corner, as England was two or three years ago. Today, Germany is considered as the country with the strongest currency in the world; a year ago, there was no talk of Germany or of her Herculean strength from the monetary point of view. Today, everybody says that Germany has the strongest monetary system because her people are hard-working and productive. As if France and England had stopped producing, and French and English workers did not want to work!
The international finance is thus putting out feelers in the world. Those wretched financiers, Mr. Chairman, are responsible for destitution throughout the world. They create destitution in all the countries of the world and not only in France or Great Britain, but even in Canada. When we have reached the point where a responsible government as the Canadian government, finds neither the courage nor the strength to act and to make a thorough reform of the Canadian monetary system, what can that government expect to do and what influence could it have at the international level?
In his article of November 20, 1968, Mr. Felteau stated:
In spite of a few considerable differences, the present situation of France is similar to that which prevails in Great Britain and which started there many years ago. This has been pointed out, for example, in the Wall Street Journal who without mincing words feels that "if Great Britain and France want to become financially respectable they will have to become financially responsible-[DOT]"
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Those are potent words: "To become financially respectable, they have to become financially responsible". Governments must become financially responsible. If the government worked toward a monetary system adapted to our physical possibilities, to the work performed by the whole nation, it could then be called financially responsible and financially respectable.
At the present time, France, Britain, Germany, the United States and Canada are not 
financially respectable but financially irresponsible, because they will not face facts. Mr. Felteau concludes by saying:
A kind of "red light" which could not by itself stabilize currencies. For this purpose nothing replaces policies of austerity.
Mr. Felteau concludes by saying that austerity must prevail, that we must tighten our belt, while production is lost or deteriorates on store shelves, and some people understand that.
I have here in my hand the letter which came with the La Presse clipping and which says:
Dear Mr. Caouette,
I hope that you will take a few seconds to talk about that on your T.V. program.
I will talk about it on television eventually, but tonight I bring the matter up in the House of Commons.
Would the Grand Charles be a Creditiste?
Because of his financial difficulties? I hope so. If we have to face financial difficulties to open our eyes, let us consider the stupidity, the nonsense of a monetary system like the one which is imposed upon the nations of the world.
What gives value to the Canadian dollar? The French people from France? The British from England? The Chinese from China? The Russians from Russia? No. Those who give value to the Canadian dollar are the Canadian people who develop their country, and no one else. Our Canadian dollars do not circulate in the United States nor in Russia.
When I went to Russia, four or five years ago, the Russian people looked at the Canadian dollar and found it funny; they did not even recognize the picture of the Queen of England. In their country, the monetary unit is the rouble. I noted, as did those who were with me, that a rouble was the equivalent of an American dollar and, as soon as we left Russia, we went to Zurich in Switzerland- I was with the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) who, at the time, was a good Social Crediter-to exchange our roubles for dollars. Then, we found that, on the international market, we needed four roubles to get one American dollar, while in Russia one rouble was equivalent to one Amercan dollar. The value of the rouble, therefore, depreciates at the international level, but does that prevent the Russians from developing at home? Some say that they will reach the moon before the Americans, and I hope so. Let them go on the moon and stay there. However, the fact remains that inside their
December 3, 1968

Finance
country, they could not care less about American dollars, Canadian dollars or French francs and they succeed in developing their country, perhaps through painstaking efforts because they do not have our production capacity. Their production system is completely disorganized, but they keep on going anyway according to their capacity.
Why, in a country such as Canada, could we not do the same thing? What prevents us from developing our riches if not a lack of money?
In the whole world, people wish to participate in the International Monetary Fund, to allow underprivileged countries to avail themselves of special drawing rights.
In my opinion, this is just running round in circles, and in twenty years from now, if we are still alive, we shall be asked to reconsider the Bretton Woods agreements, as amended according to this resolution; we shall still be contending with monetary problems that the present system cannot solve.
So, instead of contemplating a reform of the international system, let us begin with the reform of our own domestic system, let us create Canadian dollars according to the opportunities we have to develop our natural resources. At present the government wavers; claiming that we are short of money, it blocks highway construction and enlargement of hospitals, while patients are waiting for admittance.
Mr. Chairman, we will go and borrow from the International Monetary Fund to enlarge our hospitals in Canada, in the province of Quebec or Ontario; we will go and make use of special drawings rights in the International Monetary Fund to find oil wells in northern Alberta, in Saskatchewan, to enable our farmers to produce wheat and to sell it to foreign countries, or to grant them loans.
Mr. Chairman, I say we live in a financial system that defies imagination, a topsy-turvy world of fools and that we are led by the most notorious amongst them. I say and I shall never repeat enough: that is where the problem lies, and it is the duty of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the ministers, the members of government, everyone of them, to study the problem as it is, instead of indulging in vain imaginings or spinning tall tales; in short, no dreaming in colour, as the honourable member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) said the other day. He is one of those who dream in colour and has been for a long time. Indeed, he has no
solution to bring before the house; all he ever does is to mouth stupidities.

The new members of the Liberal party should remember that fact. When the leader of the Creditiste party says that there should be special drawing rights on the Bank of Canada, I certainly agree with him because if you read this morning's paper you would realize the special drawing rights which the banks have on Canadian citizens. This indicates that the banks have special drawing rights on Canadian citizens.
The substance of this bill is to set up special drawing rights within the Bretton Woods Agreement. This was agreed upon some time ago, and we are now facing its implementation. We in the New Democratic party have said that there should be an immediate conference of the members of the International Monetary Fund so that they can re-evaluate their position and bring forth some new ideas. In his introductory remarks the parliamentary secretary said this was a major step forward. If this is the only major step forward after almost 25 years, all I can say is that it is a very disappointing one. I believe we have
December 3, 1968

had many major steps backwards, and that is why we in the New Democratic party have felt that there should be a new conference of the members of the Bretton Woods Agreement to study some of the monetary problems.
When one considers the serious economic crises that have taken place in the last year and a half, such as the two onslaughts on the English pound, the pressure on the Canadian dollar followed by the crisis with regard to the French franc, he realizes that there must be some new way out of this economic chaos. It is obvious that international speculators are playing more than their full share in creating these crises, and our parliamentary leader underlined this in his statement a few days ago. He said we should do something more than what is proposed in the special drawing rights legislation. This is why we in the New Democratic party have said that serious consideration should be given to a floating exchange rate. One of the most serious problems consists in the fixing of an exchange rate to our dollar, to the pound and to the franc in the international monetary system.
So we would welcome the reference of the bill to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs so that it can be closely examined in regard to the floating exchange problem. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will invite the Postmaster General to state his views on the subject of the floating exchange rate. He is the only member in the cabinet to support it, and thus he also supports the position taken by the New Democratic party.
When the parliamentary secretary said that the approval of a substantial majority of the member nations is required, that is three-fifths of the nations having four-fifths of the total voting power, he indicated how intricate this matter is. I hope the parliamentary secretary will tell us which countries have so far given their approval to this serious matter. I suppose the over-all problem is not only to find a solution to the economic chaos which the members of the International Monetary Fund have experienced, but to examine closely the problems of underdeveloped countries, because without a great increase in trading and without the co-operation of the members of the International Monetary Fund in solving the problems of the underdeveloped nations we are found to face another serious economic crisis. Therefore I plead with the parliamentary secretary to urge the cabinet and the present Minister of Finance to press for a

new meeting of the signatories of the Bretton Woods Agreement, so they could study some of the problems which go far beyond the special drawing rights.

The resolution before the committee will allow us to introduce a bill to establish the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. The establishment of this corporation has been under discussion by the provincial governments concerned and the federal government for some time. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has had many meetings recently with the officials and ministers concerned with a view to moving forward in this important venture. The bill will enable board marketing of freshwater fish produced in the prairie provinces, the Northwest Territories

December 3, 1968
Fisheries
and northwestern Ontario to be established. It is proposed that this marketing board take the form of a crown corporation which would buy the catch directly from the fishermen, and sell the resulting fish and fish products for export and to domestic processors and distributors. This corporation would be given powers and responsibilities in interprovincial and export trade, and by agreement with the provinces it would receive under provincial legislation parallel powers and responsibilities in trade within the participating provinces. Similar arrangements would be made in the case of the Northwest Territories.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
It is intended that the corporation will conduct its operations on a self-sustaining financial basis. It will be financed by bank loans with government guarantee of repayment or by direct loans to the corporation. It will receive a grant for initial operating and establishment expenses.
The objectives of this legislation will be a more orderly marketing for the benefit of the whole fishery, and by this means the achievement of higher and more stable prices for the catch; to provide the fishermen with a better share of the market value of their fish; and to expand total sales and over-all production in the fishery.
The legislation, as I have indicated, was brought forward by the government in response to requests by the provinces concerned for assistance in dealing with the industry and its chronic problems. There were various attempts made previously to solve the problems of the industry, but they were not as successful as had been hoped. It is the conviction of the groups concerned that research activity that is designed to improve conditions in the industry will not be of full benefit unless the central problem of more orderly marketing is solved.
I might remind hon. members, Mr. Chairman, that in 1984 a federal-provincial conference established a committee to study this whole question. After this study was made, in 1985 the Mclvor commission was appointed to look into the question. The commission agreed largely with the findings of the province of Manitoba, which had also studied the matter and in which province approximately 40 per cent of the production originates.
These findings, Mr. Chairman, were that the industry is characterized by outmoded business practices and extremely heavy indebtedness on the part of the fishermen;

that low and uncertain incomes of the fishermen make it difficult for them to improve their equipment; that much of their equipment is owned by fish companies, and heavy indebtedness on the part of the fishermen to the companies gives them no choice but to sell their fish to the companies which finance them; and that for their part the companies find the provision of credit expensive and awkward. Indeed, often the companies lack the financial strength to hold their inventories until the best price can be obtained.
In its report, Mr. Chairman, the commission recommended the establishment of an export monopoly, but strongly emphasized the need for fish to be bought directly from the fishermen and for direct transfer to the fishermen of any increased export earnings. The report stressed the importance of orderly marketing, particularly in regard to exports. It recommended some concentration of processing and some streamlining of operation with regard to the flow of products to market. It urged attention be given to improving the quality of the product of the fishery in order to increase its value and reducing the risk of loss, as well as gaining wider consumer acceptance.
The Canadian inland fishery, in total, extends over an area which contains some 20 per cent or more of the world's fresh water. In this extraordinary resource, the harvesting of fish could be more immediately susceptible to scientific management than in the ocean fisheries.
In this sector, Mr. Chairman, the annual average of landings for the six year period 1960-1966 was 74.1 million pounds with a value to the fishermen of $8.5 million. Some 95 per cent of the total landings consists of white fish, lake trout, pickerel, pike and sauger. There are few alternative sources of these species in Canada or in other parts of the world, and none in equivalent volumes.
The fish referred to in this six year period produced exports valued at $13 million. These species of fish do not compete directly with markets enjoyed by ocean fish but tend to supply a specialized demand, particularly in the United States.
Some 6,000 to 7,000 fishermen obtain employment in this fishery, many of them living at near subsistence levels. A large portion of these are Indians and Metis. Under present conditions there appears to be little or no inducement for increased productivity or for men to continue in the fishery where there is other remunerative employment
December 3, 1968

available. In contrast to this there is substantial evidence that the resource possibilities of these freshwater lake areas, on a sustained yield basis, are far greater than are being exploited.
The underlying objective of the proposed legislation is to create for the fishery a totally new environment which will be attractive to capital investment and which will enable the raising of income levels of fishermen to the point where they become independently creditworthy. To achieve these objectives, Mr. Chairman, will take time and will require the support of related provincial and federal programs in the fields of education, manpower training, research, re-equipment and financing.
Following the Mclvor report, federal-provincial studies of the problems of the industry pointed to the need for collaboration between the provinces and for the use of federal powers, particularly in the regulation of interprovincial and export trade. Necessary provisions to meet these needs are made in the bill. The agency it is proposed to establish is designed in the form of a corporate organization which will receive the necessary federal powers under this legislation, and by agreement may undertake functions and responsibilities on behalf of interested provinces under related provincial legislation.
Responsibility for the administration of fisheries in these provinces is delegated under the Fisheries Act to provincial ministers. This includes matters such as licensing of fishermen. The recommendation of the provinces is that there be enforced regulations for the fishing season.
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, and because of their general economic interest in the fisheries, provincial governments have agreed to participate in the direction of the agency and, at the same time, to co-ordinate their activities in the regulation of their fisheries for their mutual benefit.
The corporation would not be intended to duplicate existing facilities of the industry. It should seek to reduce unnecessary duplication of facilities and improve efficiency by streamlining the flow of products to market. It would need to smooth over periods of peak production in order to avoid pressure on prices. Orderly marketing would be planned in consultation with the trade acting as the agents of the corporation. In planning new investment in processing, refrigerated storage, packaging and transportation fields,
Business of the House the industry would be assisted by the corporation. There are possibilities to be explored by expanding markets overseas as well as in the United States, and of increasing consumption in Canada. Greater stability could be sought in part through greater diversification of products and of markets, and through wider use of available species of fish.
As proposed by the Mclvor commission, it is intended to establish initial prices for each species, by grade, at the opening of each season, to make payment for the catch on the basis of these initial prices through the season, and at the conclusion of each season to distribute to fishermen in a final payment any additional earnings obtained through marketing of the catch. The corporation should also be empowered to extend short term credit to fishermen to finance the purchase of food and fishing supplies, following established practice in the existing industry.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-DISTRIBUTION OF PAMPHLET AS TO AVAILABILITY OF HOUSING
IMMIGRATION-DISTRIBUTION OF PAMPHLET AS TO AVAILABILITY OF HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 7 last I directed a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration which arose out of a pamphlet entitled, "Canadian Opportunities-Housing", and prepared by the Canadian government's immigration division in 1968. I asked the question because in my opinion the information in that pamphlet is, in important respects incorrect and will tend to create a completely false impression in the minds of prospective immigrants. In my opinion the pamphlet ought to be withdrawn and not used again until it is drastically revised.
Since the end of world war II more than 2 million immigrants have come to Canada. Our immigration policy has received the virtually unanimous support of all sections of the Canadian people. Business, industry, labour, have all supported this large-scale immigration. Immigrants have come to this country not only from Britain, Germany, Holland and the Scandinavian countries from which we have traditionally received them, but also in recent years from Italy, Portugal, Spain and Yugoslavia, to mention just a few. Unlike the immigrants who came here before the second world war, the vast majority of these new arrivals have gone to the cities, mainly to Toronto, Hamilton and Vancouver. They came here because it is a country in which there have been, and are, jobs, and wages which are high enough to enable them to


make the kind of living they were not able to earn in the countries from which they came. This is good, and I hope this situation will continue.
But I submit it is completely improper for the government or any other agency to misrepresent conditions in Canada. Immigrants have been told by private employers in many cases that wages are substantially higher than they really are. Within the last year, a mining company in Thompson told workers in Germany that the wages were five dollars an hour. This, of course, is not true. We do not tell immigrants about some of the difficulties they may encounter in Canada. We have not been telling them that up to this year they would not receive the benefit of the kinds of medical insurance plans which had been set up in their countries of origin, or that there is no pension plan such as exists, for instance, in Sweden.
I want to quote a couple of sections from this pamphlet. On page 14 there is one paragraph which I think is a classic of misrepresentation. It says:
In 1967, the average cost of a new house was in the neighbourhood of $19,000. The average down payment required to purchase this house was about $4,300. The average cost of an older house was approximately $12,000, perhaps a little higher in the larger cities. The average down payment for an older house was some $2,000.
It should be remembered that the majority of immigrants who come to Canada go to Toronto, Hamilton or Vancouver. I submit that there is virtually no truth in the suggestion that an immigrant or anyone else can buy a new house in those cities for $19,000, or an old house for $12,000. No government should be telling prospective immigrants that this is the situation. I suggest to the minister that this kind of thing ought to be taken out of the pamphlet immediately.
Similarly, on page 16, we find a paragraph which says:
While there has been some shortage of accommodation in Canada in the past year or so, particularly low-cost housing in the larger cities, there is at the present time an upsurge in construction which should improve conditions, particularly in the field of rentals.
Of course, the situation is not improving. It is getting worse. If this were not the case the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) who is in charge of housing would not be travelling across the country with the so-called task force looking for solutions. I could go on quoting from this pamphlet but I think I have demonstrated conclusively that some of the

statements in it are, to say the least, exaggerated. The minister ought to take steps to withdraw this pamphlet and to stop its distribution among prospective immigrants until it can be corrected.

maintopic: HOUSING-QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL LOANS TO COMBAT UNEMPLOYMENT
HOUSING-QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL LOANS TO COMBAT UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief tonight since I have partly attained the objective I had in mind when I asked the question being discussed tonight. I wish to congratulate and thank the officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for answering my request so quickly.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that a construction firm in Amos-a city located in my riding-would have been forced to lay off several construction workers during the winter if new contracts had not been forthcoming in addition to those it had yet to complete. After calling the officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, some cases were found where loans had not been accepted and were still pending, which made it possible to award to that company in Amos two housing projects. Consequently, that company will be able to keep its workers on the payroll during the winter, which will ease the unemployment situation in that region.
Indeed, as reported on page 3070 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) the following question:
Since the winter works program has been discontinued, would the hon. minister, in order to fight unemployment, allow additional loans above the 6,000 already granted to contractors for the building of houses next winter?
As will be recalled, the Minister of Transport had previously announced that loans would be available to contractors in the fall or winter, for the building of 6,000 housing units.
Once completed the houses could be put up for sale. I believe this is an excellent measure, since it meets two needs: first, in Canada, there is a strong demand for additional housing units, and I am told that not as many people as was expected or desired requested loans guaranteed or granted directly by the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation; hence the offer to finance the construction of 6,000 housing units by contractors. In the second place, this measure enables contractors taking advantage thereof to keep most of their qualified personnel during the winter season and thus fight unemployment.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that the question of the hon. member turned into congratulations to the government.
We are therefore pleased to hear that he obtained a satisfactory answer to his request, that the problems of his constituency have been solved and that the workers can con-tine to work.
As concerns housing, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that forecasts were for 175,000 housing starts during 1968. This number was subsequently raised to about 180,000. Now that the current year is about to end, it appears that this figure of 180,000 will even be surpassed, which will be an all-time record for Canada.
Housing starts during the last part of the year remained at a very high level. For instance, on October 31 of this year, 120,000 houses were being built. This figure exceeds by about 15,000 that for the same period last year. Thus, it seems obvious that we start the winter with a large number of buildings under way, and as housing starts have remained at a very satisfactory level, we can be assured that this very high level of construction will continue well into next year.

maintopic: COMMUNICATIONS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CORPORATION STRUCTURE
COMMUNICATIONS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CORPORATION STRUCTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of communications satellites is one of tremendous importance. I gather this from the minister's speeches, from Maclean's magazine, from the task forces, from the white papers, and even from a brand new ministry, the department of communications. Yet, there is a dearth of information. The minister designate seems to be somewhat less than communicative when dealing with matters relating to his own department, although he is not so reticent when discussing NATO, NORAD or matters of that kind. Some of us have sought a statement on this in the house. My question of October 18 which appears on the order paper is very simple, but it has not yet been answered.


This is a major subject. The government has declared itself to be, or to have been, seized of the question as a matter of urgency for a long time. On July 14, 1967 the then prime minister indicated that for the past year the government had been examining the Canadian space program in particular detail. Several studies on various aspects of satellite communications have been conducted under the auspices of the Department of Transport. The Chapman report was published in March under the auspices of the science secretariat. Then came the white paper a year later. There have been other announcements and indications in between. The Southam press of April 2, 1968 revealed the following:
Industry minister Drury said Monday he hoped a corporation to operate a Canadian owned domestic satellite communications system will be created by autumn.
Autumn has come and gone. The snows of winter are upon us.
Dr. Macintosh was appointed in April 1968. We have had studies, reports, rumours, magazine articles and speeches by the minister, but little in the house. We ask, why. Of course it is an important question. It is one that transcends politics; but the public should know by now the general trend and tenor of the government's policy, and the program to which the government is committing the people of this country. It is a serious question. This involves international and intra-dominion relations, and we wonder how much consultation with provinces is going to be pursued in this very important field of educational television. In the last few weeks I have noticed comments by the premier of the province of Quebec about this costly and crucial matter. These comments are very significant and very important. He has suggested that no opportunity should be missed to maximize Canadian effort in this regard.
* (10:20 p.m.)
Let us look at this, and let the people's representatives know and have a chance to discuss this vital area, which could so fundamentally affect the quality of life of the people of Canada. Have there been discussions with the provinces? Have there been discussions, with those who lead in this field, about the effect of satellites and their capacity for improvement of mankind?
Quebec is not the only province interested in educational television, but it has made moves which its leaders have publicized and which the federal government must be aware
December 3, 19G8	COMMONS
of. How does this awareness reveal itself in federal government planning? I should like to ask the minister, who is not always lacking in communication to drop and cast aside this cloak of secrecy and concealment, and let the upcoming department of communications communicate with the people of Canada through the people's tribunes, their representatives here in the House of Commons. Let us know what Dr. Macintosh thinks. I have never met him because I do not move in these exalted financial circles, as the minister does. I understand the minister graduated from McGill and that he and Dr. Macintosh are on the same basis regarding their respect for that institution. Let us know what this distinguished businessman thinks of this whole project. Let us also know if what Maclean's magazine projects in this regard is close to the truth. Tell us what the score is and what the government is recommending.
All Canadian people are involved in this costly and important matter. What could Dr. Macintosh recommend that should be concealed? I cannot envisage any way in which the Canadian satellite program could be bootlegged into an international program. What are our rights and what are our recommendations, and do these allow enough space for people to co-operate? Let us know about this very important and vital situation.
I do not know whether the minister is interested in power, but I am sure he will find that in this house of parliament knowledge is power. Surely he is aware as the minister designate of communications that he should communicate.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has made a very eloquent plea. I have the very highest regard for Dr. Macintosh. He and I were student graduates from McGill and we have

Dr. Macintosh was asked to draft a model and organizational structure of a financial and corporate satellite. As everyone in this house realizes, we have asked for a report from two companies, Northern Electric and R.C.A., as to their views regarding an appropriate kind of satellite, economically speaking, and educationally speaking, which we could send aloft. We have just received these reports. They contain many hundreds of pages of highly technical material. We must digest these reports. I would suggest to the hon. member that Dr. Macintosh's report will become relevant when the government itself has decided, in light of other technical reports, what technical progress will meet the needs of the people across this land.
This decision will have a great unifying effect in Canadian history. When Canadian needs are determined and the required facilities are evaluated we will know whether we must spend $60 million or $160 million, or something in between. This will obviously have an effect on the kind of financial structure which will evolve, and therefore will have an effect on whether we can accept Dr. Macintosh's report in its entirety.
This could be modified; but at the present time, until we have studied our needs, the facilities, the capability that is available in Canada, until we have decided on the kind of satellite that we want to send up, whether it be a Volkswagen or Cadillac type, I can make no useful recommendation to my colleagues in the cabinet. Therefore I doubt that it would be useful to table the report until I can make relevant comments on it.
